nameStory: This tiny fungus gets its scientific name from Greek words meaning 'color spore arrangement' - and the 'coerulescens' part means 'becoming blue.' When fresh, this little cup fungus often shows subtle blue-gray tints that inspired early mycologists to give it this colorful name.
description: This is a small cup fungus that forms tiny, shallow saucers on rotting wood. The cups are usually less than half an inch across and start out somewhat bowl-shaped before flattening with age. They're typically brownish or grayish with those telltale blue-gray hints when fresh, and grow in small scattered groups rather than dense clusters.

idTips.label: Blue-gray tints
idTips.description: Fresh specimens show subtle blue-gray coloration, especially around the rim of the cup - this fades to plain brown as they age

idTips.label: Cup shape
idTips.description: Forms shallow, saucer-like cups that feel thin and somewhat papery when dry, starting bowl-shaped but flattening with maturity

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Tiny cups, typically 1-10mm across - about the size of a pencil eraser or smaller

idTips.label: Growing pattern
idTips.description: Appears in small scattered groups rather than dense masses, often just a few cups clustered together

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Smooth interior surface with a slightly waxy feel when moist, becoming more papery and brittle when dried out

habitat: Found on decaying hardwood logs and branches in moist deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England. Prefers well-rotted wood that's been decomposing for at least a year or two, often in shaded areas with good humidity retention.

seasonality.spring: Early cups may appear on logs as weather warms, showing the freshest blue-gray coloration.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for finding fresh specimens, especially after periods of rain when humidity is high.
seasonality.fall: Still actively fruiting into autumn, though colors may be more faded and brownish.
seasonality.winter: Rarely active, though dried remains may persist on logs until spring.

funFact: Despite being smaller than a dime, this tiny fungus produces spores that are shot out of the cup like microscopic cannons - they can actually hear the spore discharge as tiny 'pops' if you put your ear close to a fresh specimen!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small brown cup fungi on wood, but the blue-gray tints when fresh are the key distinguishing feature. Memory trick: 'Blue clues' - look for those subtle blue hints that other small wood cups lack.
contextualKnowledge: This genus name is quite a mouthful and often mispronounced - it's 'Chrome-elo-spor-ee-OP-sis.' The 'Chromelo' part refers to the colored spore-bearing structures, which can only be seen under a microscope.
compareHints: Unlike its relative Chromelosporiopsis carnea which shows pinkish or flesh-colored tints, this species has distinctly blue-gray hues when fresh. Both are tiny wood-dwelling cups, but the color difference is reliable when you find fresh specimens.
